items.prompt: Why does a program's data survive a crash if it was written to disk, but not if it was only sitting in a regular in-memory variable?
choices: Disk is faster than RAM, so it processes the data before the crash happens
RAM is volatile — its contents depend on continuous power and vanish immediately on crash/reboot; disk (SSD/HDD) is non-volatile and retains its contents with no power at all
There's no real difference; both survive equally well
Disk data survives because the OS automatically backs it up to the cloud
items.explanation: This is the foundational distinction the whole unit builds on: volatility. RAM (including in-process variables and the OS page cache) needs continuous power; disk doesn't. Anything that only ever touched RAM is gone the instant power is lost, regardless of how the program was designed.
items.reference:
⚡ RAM

volatile — gone the instant power drops

💾 Disk

non-volatile — keeps its contents with no power

Why: anything that only ever touched RAM is gone the instant power is lost, regardless of how the program was designed.
items.learnMore:
Volatility is the whole distinction

RAM (including a process's own variables and the OS page cache) needs continuous power to hold its contents. The moment power stops, whatever electrical state represented your data is gone — there's no 'partial recovery' from that, it's simply erased.

Disk (spinning platters or flash cells) encodes data as a physical state — magnetic orientation or trapped charge — that persists with zero power. That's not an implementation detail, it's the entire reason disk exists as a storage tier separate from RAM: it trades speed for the one property RAM structurally cannot offer.

Every durability technique in this unit (fsync, write-ahead logging, group commit) exists purely to answer one question: has this data actually crossed from the volatile side to the non-volatile side yet?

items.explanation: A variable that's never written to disk exists purely in volatile memory. There is no non-volatile copy anywhere, so there is nothing for a reboot to recover — this isn't a bug or a missed setting, it's the defining property of RAM.

items.prompt: A program calls write() on a file and it returns successfully with no error. Does this guarantee the data would survive a crash happening immediately afterward?
choices: Yes — a successful write() always means the data is physically on disk
No — write() typically only guarantees the data reached the OS page cache (RAM), which is still volatile; fsync() is the call that waits for actual physical durability
Yes, but only on Windows systems
No, write() calls never actually persist data under any circumstances
items.explanation: The OS page cache is a fast, in-RAM buffer that write() typically only needs to reach to return successfully — it's a real optimization, but it means 'write() succeeded' and 'this is crash-durable' are different claims, and only fsync() closes that gap.
items.reference:
1️⃣ write() called
2️⃣ Data lands in the OS page cache (RAM)
3️⃣ ⏳ gap — crash here loses it
4️⃣ fsync() called → physically durable

Why: a successful write() only proves the data reached RAM-backed page cache, not disk.
items.learnMore:
write() is an optimization, not a promise

Operating systems buffer writes in the page cache so programs don't stall on slow physical I/O for every single write call. This is a genuinely good design — most writes never need to be that carefully durable, and forcing every one through to disk immediately would make normal file I/O unusably slow.

The cost of that optimization is that 'write() returned successfully' and 'this survives a crash right now' are two different claims. The kernel will eventually flush dirty pages to disk on its own schedule, but 'eventually' is exactly the window a crash can land in.

fsync() is the opt-out: it blocks the calling thread until the OS confirms the specific data is physically durable, converting 'probably fine' into 'guaranteed, as of this instant.'

items.prompt: Why does the OS buffer writes in a page cache instead of sending every write straight to disk?

Because physical disk I/O is comparatively slow, so buffering in fast RAM first lets write() return quickly, deferring the slower physical flush

Because page caching is only used for reads, never for writes
items.explanation: Page caching is a genuine performance optimization: most writes don't need to be durable the instant they're issued, so buffering in RAM lets programs avoid stalling on slow physical I/O for every call. The cost is that a crash can catch data still sitting only in that buffer.

items.prompt: What is the specific job of fsync(), as distinct from a plain write()?
choices: It makes the write() call itself faster
It blocks until the OS confirms the data is physically durable on disk, rather than just sitting in the fast in-RAM page cache
It compresses the data before storing it
It duplicates the write to a second, backup disk automatically
items.explanation: fsync() is the explicit durability boundary: it doesn't speed anything up (it's slower, in fact) — it waits until the disk itself has confirmed the write, converting an optimistic in-RAM write into a guaranteed durable one.
items.reference:
fsync() = "block until this data is physically confirmed durable on disk"

Why: it's the one call that turns an optimistic write into a durability guarantee — at the cost of waiting for it.
items.learnMore:
Why fsync is slow on purpose

fsync() doesn't just ask the OS to eventually flush a page — it blocks the caller until the disk hardware itself reports the write is physically committed. That round trip through the OS and the disk's own write path is real, measurable latency, typically low single-digit milliseconds even on fast SSDs.

That cost isn't a bug to optimize away — it is the durability guarantee. Any system claiming both 'instant' and 'fully durable on every write' is quietly skipping one of the two, and it's worth knowing which.

items.prompt: Why is fsync() typically noticeably slower than a plain write() call?
choices: It isn't slower — they cost exactly the same in practice
Because fsync() has to wait for the actual physical disk hardware to confirm durability, instead of returning as soon as the data reaches the fast in-RAM page cache
Because fsync() also re-reads and validates the entire file before returning
Because fsync() is implemented in a slower programming language than write()
items.explanation: The extra latency isn't overhead to be optimized away — it's the real cost of the guarantee. write() can return the moment RAM has the data; fsync() has to wait on the disk hardware itself, which is inherently slower than RAM.

items.prompt: Per the crash-timing logic in this unit, if a crash happens after write() but before fsync() was ever called, is the data recoverable after reboot?
choices: Yes, because write() already returned successfully
No — the data is still only in the volatile OS page cache at that point, so it's lost
It depends only on how large the file is
Yes, but only for text files, not binary files
items.explanation: A successful write() only proves the data reached the page cache. Without a completed fsync(), nothing has confirmed the data is on the physical disk — a crash in that window loses it, no matter how confident the write() call's success made the program feel.
items.reference:
Before write()Lost
After write(), before fsync()Lost
After fsync() returnsSafe

Why: only the row after a successfully-returned fsync is actually durable — everything before it is optimistic.
items.learnMore:
The crash-timing table is the whole unit in one row

Every durability question in this unit reduces to: where, exactly, did the crash land relative to the last successful fsync()? Before it, the data is gone. At or after it, the data is guaranteed durable — that guarantee is the entire point of the call.

A subtlety worth internalizing: a crash mid-write, with no fsync ever reached, isn't just 'the same as never having written it.' It can leave a torn, partially-written file — a distinct and often worse failure than a clean absence, because downstream code may not expect a file to be present but corrupt.

items.prompt: Why do databases fsync a small write-ahead log entry instead of fsyncing the entire (potentially large, scattered) data file on every commit?
choices: Because data files can't be fsynced at all, only logs can
Because a small, sequential log entry is cheap to fsync, so it can serve as a fast, trustworthy durability boundary while the larger data-file update is deferred safely
Because write-ahead logs don't actually need to be durable themselves
Because fsyncing a data file would corrupt it
items.explanation: The log is small and appended sequentially, which is cheap to make durable quickly — that's exactly why it can serve as the real commit point, letting the larger, slower data-file update happen afterward without weakening the durability guarantee.
items.reference:
📄 Log entry — small, sequential → cheap to fsync
🗄️ Data file — large, scattered → slow to fsync

Why: fsyncing the small log instead of the whole data file is what makes "committed" both fast and trustworthy.
items.learnMore:
The log is the promise; the data file is the implementation detail

A write-ahead log inverts the naive approach. Instead of durably updating the real data file on every commit (potentially large, scattered writes — slow to fsync), it durably appends a small, sequential description of the change to a log, and treats that as the actual commit point.

The real data file gets updated afterward, possibly much later, possibly batched with other changes. If a crash happens before that update completes, the log — which was already durable — gets replayed on restart to reconstruct exactly what should have happened. The client was never lied to: the log really was durable the instant it was acknowledged.

items.prompt: Why can the data-file update in a write-ahead-logged commit safely happen 'later, even asynchronously,' without weakening the durability guarantee already given to the client?
choices: Because data files are never actually needed for correctness

Because the log entry backing that commit is already durable on disk — a crash before the data-file update simply means replay-on-restart reconstructs it from the log, so the promise made to the client still holds
Because clients are expected to re-send transactions themselves if anything goes wrong
It can't — deferring the data-file update always risks silently losing the transaction
items.explanation: The guarantee was never 'the data file is up to date' — it was 'the log entry describing this change is durable.' Since that's already true the moment fsync returns, deferring the data-file update doesn't weaken anything; replay covers the gap.
items.reference:
📄 Log entry — small, sequential → cheap to fsync
🗄️ Data file — large, scattered → slow to fsync

Why: fsyncing the small log instead of the whole data file is what makes "committed" both fast and trustworthy.
items.learnMore:
The log is the promise; the data file is the implementation detail

A write-ahead log inverts the naive approach. Instead of durably updating the real data file on every commit (potentially large, scattered writes — slow to fsync), it durably appends a small, sequential description of the change to a log, and treats that as the actual commit point.

The real data file gets updated afterward, possibly much later, possibly batched with other changes. If a crash happens before that update completes, the log — which was already durable — gets replayed on restart to reconstruct exactly what should have happened. The client was never lied to: the log really was durable the instant it was acknowledged.

items.prompt: Per L2's group commit section, what is the actual trade-off of increasing the batch size (number of commits sharing one fsync)?
choices: There is no trade-off — a larger batch is strictly better in every way

Higher throughput (the fixed fsync cost is shared across more commits) at the cost of a larger data-loss window (more unflushed commits are at risk if a crash lands before that shared fsync completes)
Lower throughput and a smaller data-loss window, simultaneously
Batch size only affects memory usage, not durability or throughput
items.explanation: Group commit amortizes a fixed fsync cost over more commits, which is exactly why throughput scales up with batch size — but every commit in an unflushed batch is, by definition, not yet durable, so the window of at-risk data grows too. It's a genuine dial, not a free win.
items.reference:
Small batch

safer, less throughput

Large batch

faster, bigger loss window

Why: one shared fsync amortizes its fixed cost across more commits, but every commit in that batch is undurable until the one shared fsync returns.
items.learnMore:
Group commit is a dial, not a fix

fsyncing every single commit individually is correct but caps throughput at roughly 1 / (fsync latency) commits per second, regardless of how fast the CPU or the rest of the system is. Group commit buffers several pending commits and pays the fixed fsync cost once for the whole batch, which is why throughput scales up with batch size.

The trade is explicit and unavoidable: nothing in an unflushed batch is durable yet, so a bigger batch means more recently-acknowledged-as-pending work is still exposed to a crash at any given moment. Real databases expose this as a tunable (commit delay / group commit window) precisely because different workloads want different points on that curve.

items.prompt: In group commit, when is an individual commit inside a batch actually considered durable?
choices: The instant that specific commit is appended to the log buffer, before any fsync
Only once the ONE shared fsync() for the entire batch has returned successfully — every commit in the batch becomes durable at that same instant, not before
As soon as the client sends the commit request, regardless of any disk I/O
Each commit in the batch is fsynced individually; the 'batch' is purely a scheduling label
items.explanation: A batch shares exactly one fsync call. Nothing in it is durable until that shared fsync returns — every commit in the batch reaches durability simultaneously, at the moment the batch's single fsync completes, not one at a time.

faster, bigger loss window

items.prompt: Why might a newly-created file's contents be perfectly durable after fsync, yet the file itself appear to not exist at all after a crash and reboot?
choices: This can never happen; fsyncing a file's contents always guarantees the file exists too
Because the directory entry that records the file's existence at that path is separate metadata from the file's own contents, and on some filesystems it needs its own fsync to be durable
Because file contents and file existence are always stored in the exact same disk block
Because only files larger than a certain size need directory fsyncing
items.explanation: The directory entry linking a path to a file is metadata the containing directory holds, independently of the file's own bytes on some filesystems. Fsyncing only the file guarantees its contents; it says nothing about whether the directory's record of it existing is durable yet.
items.reference:
✅ File contents fsynced
❓ Directory entry pointing to the file — separate metadata, needs its own fsync

Why: "the file exists at this path" is metadata the containing directory holds, independently of the file's own bytes.
items.learnMore:
A file's existence is itself a durability claim

Fsyncing a file's contents only guarantees the bytes inside it are durable — it says nothing about whether the directory entry linking a path to that file is durable. On some filesystems those are genuinely separate pieces of on-disk metadata that can be persisted at different times.

A crash right after creating a new file can, on such a filesystem, leave the file's bytes perfectly intact on disk while the directory entry pointing to them never made it — meaning the file effectively doesn't exist after reboot, despite every byte inside it being correct. Fsyncing the containing directory after creating a new file closes this specific, easy-to-miss gap.

items.prompt: What's the fix for the 'file contents durable, but the file might not exist after a crash' gap described in this unit?
choices: Write the file's contents twice, to two different paths
Fsync the containing directory as well, after creating the new file — not just the file's own file descriptor
There is no fix; this gap is unavoidable on every filesystem
Rename the file immediately after creating it
items.explanation: Since the directory entry is separate metadata from the file's own contents, closing this gap means explicitly fsyncing the containing directory's file descriptor too, in addition to the new file's own fsync.

items.prompt: Why is a checksum on each write-ahead log entry useful for crash recovery, beyond what fsync alone provides?
choices: It isn't useful — fsync alone already prevents any possibility of a torn write
Because a crash mid-write (before fsync) can leave a truncated/garbled entry on disk; a checksum lets replay detect and stop at that corrupt tail entry instead of trusting or mishandling it
Because checksums make fsync unnecessary
Because checksums compress the log file to save disk space
items.explanation: fsync protects entries that finished being written before it was called — it says nothing about an entry a crash interrupted mid-write. A checksum gives replay a way to detect that specific torn-tail case and stop cleanly, rather than crashing on malformed data or silently accepting it.
items.reference:
📝 entry + checksum written together
🔁 on replay: checksum mismatch → stop, don't trust the rest

Why: a torn write always lands at the tail of a log — everything durably fsynced before it is still trustworthy.
items.learnMore:
Detecting corruption beats hoping it doesn't happen

A crash mid-write, with no fsync reached, can leave a log entry truncated or garbled on disk rather than simply missing. Without a way to detect that, recovery code either crashes trying to parse garbage, or worse, silently accepts corrupted data as if it were a valid commit.

Pairing each entry with a checksum of its own payload turns this into a solvable problem: on replay, recompute the checksum and compare. A mismatch means this entry (and, practically, everything after it, since a torn write happens at the tail) was never actually durably completed, and recovery should stop there rather than guess.

items.prompt: Implement `describeWriteSafety(calledFsync)`, modeling the durability claim from L3's durable-write example. If `calledFsync` is true, return the string 'durable'. If false, return 'optimistic' — matching the fact that a plain write() without fsync only reached the OS page cache.

tests.description: fsync called -> durable
fsync not called -> optimistic

items.explanation: This mirrors the exact distinction between writeWithoutFsync and writeDurably in L3: the single difference between the two functions (whether fsync was called) is the entire difference between an optimistic write and a durable one — there's no partial credit or middle state.
items.reference:
fsync() = "block until this data is physically confirmed durable on disk"

Why: it's the one call that turns an optimistic write into a durability guarantee — at the cost of waiting for it.
items.learnMore:
Why fsync is slow on purpose

fsync() doesn't just ask the OS to eventually flush a page — it blocks the caller until the disk hardware itself reports the write is physically committed. That round trip through the OS and the disk's own write path is real, measurable latency, typically low single-digit milliseconds even on fast SSDs.

That cost isn't a bug to optimize away — it is the durability guarantee. Any system claiming both 'instant' and 'fully durable on every write' is quietly skipping one of the two, and it's worth knowing which.

tests.description: single entry reconstructs correctly
later entries for the same key overwrite earlier ones
tests.expr: expect(replayLog([{ key: 'balance', value: 500 }, { key: 'balance', value: 700 }])).toEqual({ balance: 700 })

items.explanation: Both fsyncs are independently necessary: the file fsync guarantees the bytes inside it, the directory fsync guarantees the path actually resolves to that file after a crash. Either one alone leaves a real gap a crash could expose.
items.reference:
✅ File contents fsynced
❓ Directory entry pointing to the file — separate metadata, needs its own fsync

Why: "the file exists at this path" is metadata the containing directory holds, independently of the file's own bytes.
items.learnMore:
A file's existence is itself a durability claim

Fsyncing a file's contents only guarantees the bytes inside it are durable — it says nothing about whether the directory entry linking a path to that file is durable. On some filesystems those are genuinely separate pieces of on-disk metadata that can be persisted at different times.

A crash right after creating a new file can, on such a filesystem, leave the file's bytes perfectly intact on disk while the directory entry pointing to them never made it — meaning the file effectively doesn't exist after reboot, despite every byte inside it being correct. Fsyncing the containing directory after creating a new file closes this specific, easy-to-miss gap.
